title: Every Drill Bit Explained In 7 Minutes
fullText: The twist drill bit. The twist bit is the most common drill bit on the planet. Those spiraling grooves called flutes do two things at once. The cutting edge at the tip removes material and the flutes act as an exit ramp, pulling chips and dust out of the hole as you go deeper. Without that channel, debris packs into the hole and the bit either binds, overheats, or both. Twist bits work across a surprising range of materials. Wood, plastic, and light metals like aluminum are all fair game. That versatility is exactly why they are in every toolbox. But versatility comes at a cost. The tip of a standard twist bit is a simple V-shape, which means it wanders slightly when you first press it against the surface. On softwood, that wandering is usually not a problem. On metal or anything where the hole placement needs to be exact, you punch a small starter dent with a center punch first, and then the bit has somewhere to track into. One thing worth knowing is that twist bits are sized by diameter, and there are three common [music] sizing systems depending on where you are. Fractional inches in the US, millimeters in most of the rest of the world, and numbered or lettered gauges used primarily in metalworking. [music] The brad point drill bit. A brad point bit has a sharp center spur, the brad, [music] sitting at the very middle of the tip, flanked by two raised cutting edges on either side. When you press that center spur into wood, it locks the bit in place before a single flute has touched the surface. You get to choose exactly where the hole goes, and then the bit stays there. The exit hole is cleaner, too. The cutting geometry shears the wood fibers, which means the underside of the workpiece comes out smooth instead of splintered. Some brad point bits also come with a rubber depth stop collar that slides onto the shank, lets you preset how deep the hole goes, and [music] stops the bit automatically. One limitation worth mentioning is that the brad point bits are for wood. Using one on metal will destroy the tip fast. The center spur and cutting edges are not built for anything harder than timber. The masonry drill bit. Materials like concrete or brick are not just hard, they are abrasive, which means they wear the drill bit away instead of being cleanly cut by it. So, masonry bits have a tungsten carbide insert brazed into the tip. That carbide insert is crushing and scraping the material away, which is why these bits hold up where anything else would fail in seconds. The shape of a masonry bit also looks different from a twist [music] bit, even though the two look similar at a glance. The carbide tip flares out slightly wider than the shaft and the flutes are more gradual. That geometry is helpful for scooping that crushed dust up and out of the hole as it spins [music] instead of letting it pack down inside, which matters because concrete dust turns into a paste when it gets trapped. Now, for serious masonry work like running pipes through a brick wall, a standard [music] drill on rotation alone is not enough. What you need is a hammer drill or a rotary hammer. Those tools drive the bit forward and back thousands of times per minute in a hammering motion. That combination is the only practical way to get through dense concrete in a reasonable amount of time. Masonry bits also wear out faster than most other types, where that is not a defect. It is just the nature of drilling through stone. >> [music] >> The tile drill bit. Tile and masonry bits look like they belong in the same category, but they require completely different drilling approaches. A masonry bit works through percussion and force. [music] It hammers and grinds its way through. Tile, especially ceramic and porcelain, is dense and rigid, but also brittle. The hammering action of a masonry bit sends micro vibrations through the tile that the material cannot absorb, and it shatters from the inside out, [music] often well away from where the bit even touched. The tip of the tile bit is shaped like a spear or an arrowhead, and it is also tipped uh with tungsten carbide. But the cutting geometry is designed to grind away the material through rotation only, >> [music] >> with no percussion at all. Let the carbide tip do the grinding without any impact [music] force, and the tile comes through intact. One more thing worth noting. Not every tile bit works on every tile. Porcelain is denser and harder, so it requires a bit rated specifically for porcelain, often with a diamond-coated tip rather than plain carbide. The spade drill bit. A spade bit, and sometimes called a paddle bit, has a completely flat, paddle-shaped blade with a pointed spur at the center, and it is designed for drilling large-diameter holes through wood as fast as possible. The spur in the center positions the bit and stops it from walking, and the flat cutting edges on either side shear through wood aggressively. Spade bits typically range from about half an inch up to 1 and 1/2 inches in diameter, which is exactly the range where twist bits become impractical. They are the standard tool for electricians and plumbers running cables or pipes through wall studs or floor joists, anywhere you need a big hole fast, and [music] the cosmetic finish of that hole does not particularly matter. The hole saw. A hole saw is a cylindrical tube with serrated teeth around the rim, mounted on a mandrel with a pilot twist bit at the center. That pilot bit enters the material first, centers the saw, and keeps it from skating across the surface. The toothed ring then cuts a circular channel through the material, and when you pull the bit out the core sits inside the cylinder. This design makes the hole saw the right tool for large diameter holes where you need a clean precise circle rather than a rough opening. Installing a door lock set is a perfect example. Hole saws also come in a wider range of materials than almost any other bit type. Bi-metal hole saws cut wood, thin metal and plastics. Diamond coated versions handle stone, carbide tipped versions cut through harder materials. One practical tip, the circular core that gets punched out tends to get jammed inside the cylinder. There's usually a slot or a small hole in the side of the saw for exactly this reason. A screwdriver through that slot levers the core out. The step drill bit. The step bit looks like a miniature chrome Christmas tree and it is one of the cleverest designs in the drill bit world because it does the work of a dozen different bits in one tool. The cone-shaped body has a series of stepped diameters machined into it, each slightly wider than the one below. Starting at the tip, the bit enters the material at a small diameter and as you push deeper each step up cuts a slightly larger hole. You can produce any hole size from the smallest step to the largest with a single bit depending only on how far you drive it. They also work in softwood and plastic but sheet metal is where they earn their place. One detail that matters when buying is that cheaper step bits have the steps ground into the body without any separation between them. Better step bits have a flat land at each step which is what allows each diameter to cut cleanly rather than just deforming the edge of the hole as it passes through.
